Yes, that was the same year as the Goodman band.
It wasn't any relationship.
No, no, that was John Hammond's production.
I was going to ask you about John Hammond, because he seemed to also have the concert idea. Was that the concert idea of producing jazz?
That was a swing production, you know. Those were common.
They were?
Yeah, I mean, that was being done anyway.
Earlier than 1936?
Yes, earlier than the Carnegie Hall thing. But I was bringing real jazz men into Carnegie Hall, and to Symphony Hall in Boston, and I did a concert in Hollywood Bowl, and in general had some...
Who did you bring to Carnegie Hall?

Carnegie Hall. That was Muggsy Spanier, Sidney Bechet, Joe Sullivan, Pops Foster, Baby Dodds. The same group that I brought on my Ivy League tour when we toured the Ivy League schools. You know, showing jazz to the music departments, where I would do a little lecture and illustrate it with music.
Who... Now, when you were approached at Temple to do a concert, why were you approached?
Well, because I was the only one who knew anything about it. I had a collection of records, for example, that everybody knew.
Oh, I see.
You see. I see. And besides that, it was known that I was from New Orleans.
When did you start collecting the records, or did you get them from your...
I always had them. I just don't know.
I'm wondering if you mentioned your uncle had always collected them or something, or... Yeah. ...that it came down to your family?
Yes, of course. Another thing is that I knew musicians...
You took them to Temple with you?
Yeah, sure.
Oh, in 78?

That's right, yeah. Because, well, there was nothing else to take. And all those... See, there are a lot of musicians that the family just hired from time to time, like to go out to Millenburg for a picnic. I mean, we'd hire Papa Celestan's band, you know. And so I knew all the musicians. I've known, for example, Jeanette Kimball, who plays the piano in Papa Celestan's band. I've known her since I was five years old. And so, you know, having grown up with a musician like that, I mean, a musician was never anything exotic to me.

It seems to me that, you know, in a sense you're in a class of people. When I put Hammond in with you, to a certain extent you may disagree with me. But these people, like yourself and Hammond, that started producing jazz concerts, were also interested in record collecting, or maybe, you know, or at least had a lot of records.
Usually.
And the phenomenon of record collecting here seems to be very important.
Well, in the first place, you have to be interested in some kind of music.
Yeah. Or preserving, too, a certain kind of music.
Well, I don't think that ever occurred to me in those days, because it never occurred to me that it was in danger.
Yeah.

I never thought of there being anything to preserve yet, you see. There was no reason to think in those terms. And besides that, I hadn't done yet a lot of the theoretical thinking that I have done since, which is understandable. But I think that the first thing that's necessary is that you feel a need for the music. And then you feel a need to share the music with other people who are interested in what you've got, you see. And you realize that they don't have the opportunity to listen. And of course, in those days, we didn't have any such thing as tape recorders, that you'd be able to run off items from your collection for other people. But other people wanted to hear the music, you see. So I just got concerts together, really, for them.
Mm-hmm.
And of course, there were enough of them at the time to fill the houses.
Mm-hmm.

And then when I would go someplace like Chicago or St. Louis, I would work with whoever was the disc jockey that had the jazz audience. And we would co-produce, like Dave Garroway in Chicago or Rush Hughes in St. Louis, that kind of thing. And I worked out a little route, you know, for jazz bands. Mm-hmm. And everybody has worked for me. Mm-hmm. And there was also even a time when I had a foray into bebop, because there were so many of the people who were interested in the music that I was producing that started to talk to me about doing some of the new stuff and giving the people an opportunity to hear that, because they didn't have any chance to hear that in Philadelphia.
Mm-hmm.

And the first concert I brought in, in fact, for them, in fact, the only time when I actually ever produced a bebop concert, which I did not produce under my own name, but which featured Lenny Tristano and Fats Navarro and Billy Bauer and certain other musicians whose activity was significant at that time. You asked about Miles Davis before. Mm-hmm. I met Miles Davis in Philadelphia, too. And I met him, there was a fellow by the name of Nat Siegel, who was a small, he owned a club called the Downbeat, where these musicians got together and met. And he invited me over there one time to discuss a major concert, which would include both their kind of music and my kind of music, and Miles Davis was playing in his place that night. And that was the first time that I met him. And I, as a matter of fact, I had never heard of him before. I didn't even know what instrument he played. And when, when I sat down at the table with Nat, I didn't even know that he was one of the musicians. But we talked for a while. And then, after having talked for a while, he got up and he played. And I realized that what he was playing was nothing that I could, could produce for my audience.
Mm-hmm.

And I wasn't sure that I wanted, at that time, I wasn't sure that I wanted any identification with it at all. But I was interested to hear what he was doing. And so when he came back to the table, I talked to him about it again. And I asked him some questions because I was genuinely curious to know what had led him into this strange approach to music. And I found him to be literally unable to express himself verbally. And after that, I met him other times, you know, because when you're around with musicians, other musicians come in. I met him a couple of times in Birdland. And I met him in Mittens. And I met him in the Village Vanguard.
And so when you say hello, you know. Do you think he's a great musician?
Oh, no. I don't think that he is of really any musical consequence at all.

You have some fairly, I don't know whether unorthodox or what, but views on some musicians. For instance, there's probably no doubt in most people's minds that they're interested in jazz. If they agree with all the people, they're supposed to know something about it. Duke Ellington is one of the great, great American music makers.
Yeah, well, that's a great American myth.
You have a completely different view of Duke Ellington. That's true. Can you just explain a little bit? Yeah, well. I think it's interesting.

Well, I think that it's interesting that Duke Ellington has developed the reputation that he has. Really, it's an indictment of the criteria of the American public that he is accepted as being a great musical genius. One thing is, of course, that so far as I am able to determine on the basis of what I would consider to be reasonable investigation, first, that he was not, in fact, a composer, that he never really composed anything at all of any significance, certainly none of the things with which his name is identified, that we already know who was responsible for the successful things. We know here in New Orleans, certainly we know that Lorenzo Teo wrote Mood Indigo some eight years before...
Jimmy Noon's solo became the Creole Love Call. Yes. Jimmy Noon's solo in one of the King Oliver pieces.
That's right, became the Creole Love Call. The sophisticated lady, of course, lock, stock, and barrel is Otto Hardwicks. The arrangements were made by...
But isn't, Al, let me ask you this, isn't that the definition of a jazz composer to a certain extent, that he does draw upon his musicians in a way?

Well, it's not a question of drawing upon his musicians. It's the fact that he has literally used their material, you see? And the music is published with their names on it. It's not as though Ellington removed their identification. No, I mean, the point is that it says, sophisticated lady, Otto Hardwick and Duke Ellington. Unfortunately, I mean, it's not unethical for Ellington to have his name on it. That's not what I'm suggesting.
Okay.

Or that his name appears with Barney Begard's on Mood Indigo, which Barney Begard had nothing to do with the composition of that either. Take the A train, says Hodges Ellington. This is all true. But what I'm saying is that in none of these cases did Ellington make any contribution to the composition. These were all compositions of these various people. Now, because of slick publicity, he has been presented as a great creative genius who has composed all these pieces.
But it's not just slick publicity, Al. It's people like Gunther Schuller who in their book, Early Jazz, call him the first great composer.

Well, they need to have done a little more investigating than they did. But apparently, he doesn't know what actually took place in these things. And if he were to investigate it even superficially, he would find that these things are true.
Now, didn't he write a lot of songs, though?
Who, Ellington?
Yeah.
None that I'm able to discover that he actually wrote. Or even that he actually contributed to.
Well, what did he do?
Well, what he did was to present the material to audiences, which he did very well.
Did he? How? What do you mean?
Well, I mean, he could sit at a piano and smile.
Right.
And he could get up on a microphone and make comments that were pleasing to people.

Wasn't he good at drawing out the best in his musicians? For instance, many of whom were New Orleans musicians. Wasn't he talented in the way he placed them and in the way in which he brought them out to their course?

I don't think so. I don't think he contributed to that. I think that whoever happened to be functioning as concertmaster and as man, and I think that whoever happened to be doing the arrangements were the people who were responsible for that. And he did have great people. You see, there's no question about that. But the fact that he had great people does not make him a great composer. He was certainly not a great musician. I think even his closest associates would agree to that. And that his major contribution was his inability to front a band. However, this is not what he's famous for. He's famous for things that he couldn't do. And I consider that a sad commentary on the general public and its willingness to accept. And even the critics like Gunther Schuller and so on who make statements like that without a genuine understanding of what happened.
Well, of course, Gunther Schuller wrote a whole book on musical development.
Yeah, I try to forget it.

Okay. Let me ask you about another jazz great who's of particular interest to me, and that's Charlie Parker. I know that you've had dealings with him in your own recording industry to a certain extent of work. Yeah. But would you say that Charlie Parker's a great musician?

No. No. I would say that Charlie Parker was a musician who developed high skills in doing particular things that were of interest to him. But I wouldn't say that he was a great musician. Certainly not that. I would say that his music is, of course, largely influenced by Rudy Valli, according to...
And this is something I don't quite understand.
Well, I would have to refer you to Charlie Parker himself on that subject, and he expanded it considerably in Downbeat. So if you look in the Downbeat Index, you'll find Charlie Parker himself.
Did he say he likes Rudy Valli? No, no.
No, he says that he did everything he could to make it possible for himself to sound like...

But jazz musicians are always notorious. Like Fats Waller plays... I said he played organ, and he liked some organ player. He did like... Who was the most smeltsy organ player in the world. And there was no way by listening to Fats Waller's music that you were going to say... Yes. ...that he was influenced by that organ.

Well, what I am saying is that if you listen to Rudy Valli, and especially to Dick Stabile on records... Yeah. And if you listen to them... You're going to hear all those fast changes that Parker makes? You're going to hear all those things that Parker makes. I don't believe it. Well, try it and see. I don't believe that. I recommend that you try it and see. Yeah. Because it'll be illuminating for you to do that. And I considered that Charlie Parker was very pleasant. He had a tendency to be narcissistic. He was friendly but unresponsive to people around him. He smiled a lot. He was very cooperative, certainly. And I considered him to be a pleasant personality. The music that he played never did interest me at all. And what he did mainly was to play with the medium. And I believe that it's necessary for somebody to do more than that in order to be a great artist. That is, that unless the artist is expressing his own reactions to the world and to the society in which he lives, in his medium, that his stuff can only then be of value as exercises.
I hear a lot of protest in Charlie Parker.
Yeah, of course. I hear protest, too. But I believe that it's unfocused.
He apparently was very conscious of the racial question.

Well, that's what I kept hearing all the time. But it never seemed to manifest itself in actual relationships. As a matter of fact, I considered that there was less of that in Charlie's personality than in most of the musicians that I know. He was perfectly prepared to take any individual on his face value, regardless of his color. And I don't think that he felt oppressed by being black. Certainly no more than other musicians have. Like, I know black musicians who, for instance, won't eat fried chicken or watermelon in public because they are self-conscious about the black image. You see? And, of course, I deplore this circumstance. I deplore the image and I deplore their self-consciousness about it. But Parker didn't seem to have that kind of attitude toward things. He really seemed to be prepared to do anything he wanted to do. And he seemed extremely relaxed and easy.
Are there any musicians that do not relate so much to the New Orleans style that you are particularly impressed by or with? Yeah, of course.

I was much impressed with Lips Page, whom I consider to be a great individual artist. I was impressed with Lucky Roberts, who's, I suppose, not only because of his music, but because of the environment of that place and that time. I was, of course, impressed with Pee Wee Russell, whom I was very fond of personally. That's a guy that I always enjoyed having around. And, of course, these are not New Orleans folks. I like, there were a lot of musicians that I liked personally, whose music I didn't like at all, which is even more common. But I consider that there were a lot of great musicians that weren't from New Orleans, like Hody's, for example.
You are Hody's?

Mm-hmm. And there are musicians like Bobby Hackett, for example, who's spectacular, but whose approach to music doesn't, I don't respond to emotionally at all. It's not my kind of thing. Although I respect him and his work.
For the same reason, you don't respond to Big Spider?
Yes, very much the same reasons. He was influenced. Yeah. So, I would say that there were quite a lot of musicians that I enjoyed.
Of course, some of them. But the great ones you weren't impressed by at all.
That's a good line.
And, okay, what, let me just ask you this before we close, because we're getting close. Who have you closely worked with that you've particularly been impressed by?
Oh, Johnny Wiggs. I consider Johnny Wiggs to be the most competent musician I ever knew.
Nobody knows who Johnny Wiggs is.
Unfortunately. I've done my best.
But I might mention that Johnny Wiggs was the teacher of Charlie DeVore.
And also of Pete Fountain, Jack Delaney, George Gerard.
But for me, Charlie DeVore is a particular interest because he plays in the Hall Brothers band in Mendota.
Right.
And so it makes a connection to my home territory. But he was also a teacher of Pete Fountain.
Yeah, of course.
And he's a New Orleans-based person. He never left New Orleans.
Oh, he did, sure.
For any extended period of time?
Oh, yes, yes. He certainly did. He worked in New York. He worked in vaudeville bands.
Is there one musician in particular you've worked the most with in your recording career?
Let's see. Gee, I'd have to stop and think about that. I mean, like, Danny Barker's made a lot of records with me.
I'd say outside of New Orleans.
Outside of New Orleans? Dan Burley. Of course, Danny Barker outside of New Orleans, too. Pops Foster.
Uh-huh.
And I could never get away from New Orleans rhythm people, for one thing. And it's hard to think of who was the most.
Did you know Wellman Broad at all?
Oh, sure. Bro.
Bro?
Bro. Yes, I knew him very well.
He did wonders for Duke, didn't he?
He certainly did, yeah. He was great. One of the greatest of the bass players.
And you've done stuff with Sidney Bache quite a bit, I would say.
I never recorded Sidney Bache.
Oh, you never did record?
No. I knew him well, and I did a lot of concerts with him, and we traveled together, but I never made a record.
Oh, you never made a record.
No. Chips never fell that way. Okay. We must be to the end.
Yeah. We're getting in there. Okay. Well, if it looks like we could do some more, we'll do some more. All right. Something like that.
It could be productive. You probably don't usually get into this much theory with anybody. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
